title: Architecture (for contributors)
text: Architecture for contributors This page explains how easy-math-lang is put together, so you can find your way around before touching code. End users should start with the Installation guide installation.md and Writing math algebra.md . <!-- toc --> - The big picture the-big-picture - The compiler src/compiler/ the-compiler-srccompiler - Entry points entry-points - What one compile does what-one-compile-does - Module map module-map - Geometry src/geometry/ geometry-srcgeometry - Language server src/lsp/ language-server-srclsp - Desktop editor src/editor/ desktop-editor-srceditor - Tests tests/ tests-tests - CI and releases .github/workflows/ ci-and-releases-githubworkflows - Where to change what where-to-change-what - The five packages in plain words the-five-packages-in-plain-words - See also see-also <!-- /toc --> New to the project? Read Contributing ../CONTRIBUTING.md first for the setup steps — then come back here. --- The big picture One .ezmath text file in, one PDF or image/HTML/Typst file out: Five packages under src/ — all plain Python packages, imported as compiler. , geometry. , lsp. , editor. , typst_bundle. : | Package | What it does | Entry point | |---|---|---| | src/compiler/ | .ezmath → Typst → PDF/images the whole language | easy-math-lang → compiler.pipeline:main | | src/geometry/ | draw blocks: parse rules → solve positions → draw CeTZ | called by the compiler | | src/lsp/ | Language server: errors, completion, hover, outline | easy-math-lsp → lsp.server:main | | src/editor/ | Desktop editor PySide6 | easy-math-editor → editor.app:main | | src/typst_bundle/ | Vendored Typst packages: pinned versions + import line + bundle resolution | stdlib-only leaf; used by geometry and compiler | The single most important rule: there is exactly one parser. The language server and the editor's preview both drive the same compiler modules — never fork the syntax into a second implementation. --- The compiler src/compiler/ Entry points - main pipeline.py — the CLI: parses --format/--ppi/-o/--strict/… and calls: - compile_ezmath input, output, … pipeline.py — the public API. The editor preview, the tests, and the CLI all call this. It is wrapped by @_with_diag_count , which counts Error / Warning writes only at the start of a line, so echoed source lines in the new context blocks never count and implements --strict . What one compile does 1. Read + strip comments — comments.strip_comments protects URLs and \ … \ math ranges from // . 2. Line loop compile_ezmath — every line is classified: fenced blocks, math-mode continuations, friendly statements let x = 5 , define ... , single-line and block draw ... , silent blocks ... , assignments <x> = ... , doc_title / doc_font control lines, friendly blocks headings, lists — and finally normal text. 3. Per-line text pipeline — _render_text_line runs a fixed sequence of phases on each ordinary line each phase is one small module : p ... raw segments → <variables> → undefined check → defines → calc → \ … \ math pairs → det /tables → plot → styling/ image → math commands → unknown-command warnings → pi / infinity → merge math → subscripts → symbol shortcuts → multiplication symbol → escape to Typst. 4. Typst generation — adds set text/page/document , joins lines, writes doc.typ , and records a source map doc.smap.json so the editor can jump from a PDF position back to your source line. 5. Failure gates — an unclosed block or a broken draw stops the build before Typst runs everything else only warns . 6. Export — _run_typst_export passes the vendored Typst bundle as package_path when present and calls typst.compile for PDF/PNG/SVG/HTML or copies the .typ for typ exports , then intermediate files are cleaned up unless --save-build-artifacts . Module map | Module | Responsibility | |---|---| | pipeline.py | Everything above: line loop, per-line phases, Typst output, CLI | | state.py | CompileContext — per-run state variables, defines, doc title/font, plot counters, original source lines f

Delete it and type your own math, or open an example instead: File → Open → examples/example.ezmath . - On first run a dismissible welcome banner shows a 3-step quick start and a button that opens a ready-to-run example. It can be reopened from Help → Welcome ; tick "Don't show again" to keep it away. When the editor is empty it also shows a faint hint pointing to Help → Examples and the symbol bar. - Press Ctrl+B or Build → Compile to turn the document into a PDF. The status bar tells you where the PDF was written. - If a document has unsaved changes, the window title shows a and you will be asked before closing. --- Language English / Vietnamese - The editor interface is available in English default and Vietnamese vi . On first run the language follows your system locale for example LANG=vi_VN.UTF-8 ; afterwards your choice is remembered. - Change it any time with View → Language… English, Vietnamese, or System default . The change applies immediately, without touching your document, cursor, or open files, and is persisted in ~/.config/ezmath/config.ini as ui/language . - Only UI chrome is translated. Language syntax and keywords vec , draw , point , … , file names, code snippets, and compiler/LSP identifiers are never translated. Command descriptions and draw titles are translated by name/id symbol.<name>.description , draw.<id>.title ; the registry data itself stays canonical English and the UI looks the translation up at display time. - Qt has no Vietnamese catalog, so Qt-generated texts are set explicitly from the catalog: text-edit context menus editor/qt_text.py , standard dialog buttons, file dialog labels file dialogs are always Qt-drawn, never native, so their labels can be translated , and input dialog buttons. The font dialog's internal labels cannot be set this way and stay Qt-generated see remaining exceptions in scripts/audit_i18n_allowlist.json and below . - UI fonts prefer Noto Sans / DejaVu Sans, which render Vietnamese diacritics correctly; Qt

title: Exporting to PDF, images, HTML and Typst
text: Exporting to PDF, images, HTML and Typst easy-math-lang writes the intermediate Typst source doc.typ next to your .ezmath , converts it with the typst package, then removes the intermediates on success — only the deliverable stays. Pick the output by extension — or explicitly with --format . Quick examples typst is accepted as an alias of typ --format typst , out.typst , matching the "Typst" label used in the docs and the editor. The installed binaries easy-math-lang , ezmath accept the same flags. In the desktop editor: File → Export As… PDF/PNG/SVG/HTML/Typst works for saved and untitled documents; PNG prompts for DPI default 150 . Formats | Format | Extension | Notes | |---|---|---| | PDF | .pdf | Default. Print-ready A4 document. | | PNG | .png | Raster image. --ppi 1..1200 controls resolution. | | SVG | .svg | Vector image scales cleanly for slides/web . | | HTML | .html | Single web page Typst HTML export . | | Typst | .typ .typst also works | Intermediate source only — no typst.compile call. | Multi-page images PNG/SVG are one-file-per-page when the document spans pages. doc.png with 3 pages writes doc-1.png , doc-2.png , doc-3.png the CLI prints the stem-{p}.ext pattern . To choose the pattern yourself, include {p} in the output name: out-{p}.png . Tips - Unknown extensions e.g. out warn and assume PDF — add --format to be explicit. - Invalid --format / --ppi fails fast with exit code 2 and a hint. - Intermediates .typ , .smap.json , -plot- .svg next to the input are removed on success; pass --save-build-artifacts to keep them for debugging layout. Failures always keep them. The compile_ezmath API and the editor preview always keep them. image files are your own sources, never intermediates: they are never deleted, and typ / html exports to another folder copy them along preserving their relative layout so the exported source keeps working. - Geometry draw renders identically in every format CeTZ canvas . See also - Troubleshooting and FAQ troubleshooting.md — where did my PDF go? which messages mean what? - Cheat sheet cheatsheet.md — quick reference for everyday commands - Glossary glossary.md — PPI, intermediates, exit codes explained Honest status and --strict A document with Error diagnostics undefined <variable> , calc division by zero, … still writes the PDF by default and exits 0 for backward compatibility — but the final line is honest: instead of Successfully compiled … via Typst! clean builds keep the success message . The PDF may contain inline markers like Calc Error: … where evaluation failed. Pass --strict to turn errors into a non-zero exit the PDF is still written when possible : Useful in CI to fail a build on typos and bad calculations.

title: Drawing Geometry
text: Drawing Geometry easy-math-lang can draw geometric figures — triangles, circles, angles, and more — directly in your PDF. <!-- toc --> - How it works how-it-works - A simple example a-simple-example - Points points - With exact coordinates with-exact-coordinates - Without coordinates auto-positioned without-coordinates-auto-positioned - What auto-placement decides and what it doesn't what-auto-placement-decides-and-what-it-doesnt - Construction points construction-points - Picking an intersection picking-an-intersection - When things go wrong when-things-go-wrong - Lines lines - Line segment from A to B line-segment-from-a-to-b - Infinite line infinite-line - Ray starts at A, goes through B ray-starts-at-a-goes-through-b - Triangles triangles - Circles circles - Arcs arcs - Angles angles - Right angle 90° marker right-angle-90-marker - Rules and constraints rules-and-constraints - Distance between two points distance-between-two-points - Perpendicular lines 90° angle perpendicular-lines-90-angle - Parallel lines parallel-lines - Point lies on a line point-lies-on-a-line - Point lies on a circle point-lies-on-a-circle - Two sides have the same length two-sides-have-the-same-length - Two angles are equal two-angles-are-equal - Midpoint midpoint - Intersection of two lines intersection-of-two-lines - Labels and measurements labels-and-measurements - Examples examples - Example 1 — Right triangle example-1--right-triangle - Example 2 — Isosceles triangle example-2--isosceles-triangle - Example 3 — Circle with a tangent line example-3--circle-with-a-tangent-line - Tips tips - See also see-also <!-- /toc --> You don't need to know the exact coordinates of every point. Just describe the relationships between points e.g. "these two sides are equal", "this angle is 90°" , and the program figures out where to place everything automatically. --- How it works You write geometry commands inside a draw ... block. The program: 1. Reads your commands 2. Calculates where each point should go using a constraint solver 3. Draws the figure and places it in your PDF --- A simple example This draws triangle ABC where you have set the coordinates yourself. > Friendly: , works like ; between points > triangle A, B, C = triangle A ; B ; C , > line A, B , intersection C, line A, B , line D, E . > When ; is present it wins. point A = 0, 0 never splits — > its x, y comma is coordinates, not a separator. --- Points A point is a dot with a name. With exact coordinates If you know where a point should be, write its position as x, y : Think of it like a grid — x goes right, y goes up. Without coordinates auto-positioned If you don't know or don't care about the exact position, just name the point. The program will place it automatically based on the other rules you give: This is useful when you say something like "C is 3 cm from A" — the program figures out a position for C that satisfies the rule. What auto-placement decides and what it doesn't A point without coordinates is placed by the solver from the constraints that mention it. Four things to know: - Position and rotation are arbitrary unless you pin them. An auto-positioned figure can land anywhere, at any rotation. For a tidy, canonical picture, pin the first points yourself — point A = 0, 0 and, to fix the orientation, point B = 4, 0 — and let the solver place the rest. - The result is deterministic. The same block always produces the same figure: auto points start from a fixed guess there is no randomness , so re-running a file never moves the points. - The solver is numeric, not exact. Lengths and angles come out right to about 1% in our checks a 3-unit leg landed within 0.03 and a 5-unit side within 0.05 — plenty for a drawing, but don't treat the output as a mathematical proof. - Constraints must determine the figure. A point that no constraint mentions is placed arbitrarily, and too few constraints can collapse a shape a bare triangle A ; B ; C over three auto points draws A and C almost on top

title: Getting started
text: Getting started Write your first ezmath file in 5 minutes. This tutorial walks you through creating a .ezmath text file and turning it into a PDF. No programming experience needed — if you can type in Notepad, TextEdit, or VS Code, you can do this. --- Step 0 — Install easy-math-lang You need the easy-math-lang command on your computer. Fastest way no Python needed : download the installer for your system from the Releases page https://github.com/duo8097/easy-math-lang/releases : - Windows: EasyMathLang-Windows-x64-Setup.exe - macOS Apple Silicon : EasyMathLang-macOS-arm64.dmg - Linux: .deb , .rpm , or Arch package Install it, then launch Easy Math Editor from your Start Menu or Applications. > Need step-by-step install help? See the Installation guide installation.md . --- Step 1 — Create your first .ezmath file Open any text editor Notepad, TextEdit, VS Code, anything and type: Save it as my-doc.ezmath in a folder you can find again for example your Desktop or Documents folder . What each line means | Line | What it does | |------|--------------| | // My first ezmath document | A comment — anything after // is ignored and never shows in the PDF | | doc_title My Lesson | Sets the document title and the PDF's metadata | | <width> = 5 | Creates a variable named width and gives it the value 5 | | <height> = 3 | Creates a variable named height with value 3 | | <area> = calc <width> <height> | Calculates 5 × 3 = 15 and stores it in area | | The rectangle is ... | Normal text — printed as-is in the PDF | | <width> , <height> , <area> | Variables are replaced by their values when the PDF is built | Rule of thumb: words in <...> are variables you define. Words starting with are commands that do something special. Everything else is ordinary text. --- Step 2 — Compile it to PDF Open a terminal in the folder where you saved my-doc.ezmath and run: If you installed from source, use uv run easy-math-lang my-doc.ezmath instead. You should see: A file named my-doc.pdf now sits next to my-doc.ezmath . Open it — you should see: > My Lesson > > The rectangle is 5 cm wide and 3 cm tall. > Its area is: 5 . 3 = 15 cm² --- Step 3 — Try more math Change your file to this: Save and compile again: The PDF now shows the triangle area 12 , a real fraction ½ , x², √x, and π. --- Step 4 — Draw a simple figure ezmath can draw geometry too. Add this at the end of your file: This describes a triangle: point A at the bottom-left, point B to the right, point C above the middle. ezmath figures out where everything goes and draws it in your PDF. > You describe relationships points, distances, angles and the > program figures out the exact coordinates. Full guide: > Drawing geometry geometry.md . --- Step 5 — What if something goes wrong? You might see a message like: This means ezmath found <widht> but you never defined it — probably a typo you meant <width> . The message shows the line number and the exact spot, so you can fix it and compile again. Every message points at a spot in your .ezmath file. Full list of messages and fixes: Troubleshooting and FAQ troubleshooting.md . --- You're done! In 5 minutes you: 1. Installed easy-math-lang 2. Wrote a .ezmath file with variables and calculation 3. Compiled it to a PDF 4. Tried fractions, powers, roots, and π 5. Drew a triangle What next? - Cheat sheet cheatsheet.md — everything you type most often, on one page - Writing math algebra.md — every command explained, with examples - Desktop editor editor.md — the graphical editor with shortcuts and panels - Glossary glossary.md — every term explained in plain language

title: Glossary
text: Glossary Plain-language meanings of the words used in these guides — no programming background assumed. > Reading a message from the compiler? Jump to > Troubleshooting and FAQ troubleshooting.md . --- For writing documents .ezmath file The plain-text file where you write your document. Any text editor works Notepad, TextEdit, VS Code, or the built-in desktop editor editor.md . Argument A value you pass to a command, inside its parentheses. In frac 2 ; 3 the arguments are 2 and 3 . Arguments are separated by ; — or by , if you prefer. Calc — short for calculation . The calc ... wrapper makes the compiler do arithmetic for you: calc 2 + 3 becomes 5 . Without it, text is printed exactly as you wrote it. Comment A note for yourself that never appears in the PDF. Start it with // . Define — define name = value . A name that stands for a value. The name is printed exactly as written — it is not calculated. See Variables vs defines algebra.md variables--storing-calculated-values . Variable — <name> = value . Like a define, but it can be calculated <area> = calc <width> <height> and its value updates everywhere you use <name> . Silent block — ... around variable definitions so they are computed but not printed in the PDF. Math mode — an expression wrapped in backslashes, like \ x = 2 \ . Inside it you get proper math typography fancy fonts, automatic spacing without needing LaTeX. Symbol shortcut — a short text spelling that becomes a symbol in the PDF, like <= → ≤ or alpha → α. Separator — the character between arguments ; or , and rows | . When ; is present it wins, so 100,000 stays one number. --- For the output PDF — the finished, printable document the compiler produces. PNG / SVG — image formats you can export instead of PDF. PNG is a picture made of pixels good for slides ; SVG is vector stays sharp at any size . Multi-page documents produce one file per page. HTML — a web-page version of your document. Typst — the typesetting engine that turns text into a beautiful PDF. easy-math-lang writes a small Typst file for you behind the scenes and hands it over — you never need to learn Typst. It is installed automatically; see Installation installation.md . PPI DPI — pixels per inch; the sharpness of an exported PNG. Higher = sharper and bigger. --ppi 300 is print quality. Intermediate files — the temporary .typ file, source map .smap.json , and -plot- .svg diagrams created during a build. They are deleted after a successful build; pass --save-build-artifacts to keep them for debugging. Source map — a record of where each generated line came from in your .ezmath file, so errors and editor links can point back to the right line. --- For the tools Terminal / command prompt The window where you type commands instead of clicking buttons. Also called "Console", "PowerShell", or "Shell". CLI — command-line interface ; running easy-math-lang from the terminal as opposed to clicking in the editor editor.md . uv — the tool that installs Python packages for this project. You only need uv sync once, then uv run ... to run things. See Installation installation.md . Compiler — the program that reads your .ezmath file and produces the PDF easy-math-lang . LSP / language server — easy-math-lsp , a helper that gives your editor autocompletion, hover info, and live error checking for .ezmath files. See Language server lsp.md . Diagnostic — a message the compiler prints about your document. Two kinds: Error something is wrong, e.g. an undefined variable and Warning suspicious but the build continues . Messages often appear inside the PDF too, exactly where the problem is. Strict mode — the --strict flag: instead of writing the PDF and exiting with code 0, the compiler exits non-zero when there were errors — useful in automated builds CI so typos fail loudly. Exit code — the number a program returns after running: 0 means success, anything else means something went wrong scripts and CI read this . --- For developers Pipeline — the ordered steps the co

Download EasyMathLang-Windows-x64-Setup.exe from the latest stable release on the GitHub Releases page https://github.com/duo8097/easy-math-lang/releases or the nightly artifact under Actions -> "Build Installers" . 2. Run it and follow the steps. Two options are offered: - Create a desktop shortcut off by default . - Add compiler/LSP to PATH off by default — tick this only if you want to run easy-math-lang from a terminal. It appends to your user PATH HKCU\Environment , so no extra permissions are needed for that step. 3. Launch Easy Math Editor from the Start Menu. No further setup is needed: the editor finds its helper programs easy-math-lsp , easy-math-lang next to itself automatically — see Desktop editor editor.md under-the-hood-helper-programs . The editor and the helpers all install into one folder, C:\Program Files\EasyMathLang\bin\ , which also holds the single shared library directory _internal\ installed as bin\_internal\ . The executables load their runtime from bin\_internal\ ; keep that folder next to the .exe files. --- Option A2 — macOS disk image easiest Apple Silicon only M1 or newer ; requires macOS 14 Sonoma or newer; does not run on Intel Macs or on macOS 13 Ventura . 1. title: Language server (editor support)
text: Language server editor support The file easy-math-lsp is a Language Server Protocol https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/ server for Easy-Math-Lang. Connect a compatible editor to it and you get, while you type: - Error messages — undefined variables with "did you mean …?" hints , broken calc ... expressions, unknown commands, and geometry problems - Autocompletion — your variables and defines, built-in math commands frac , sum , … , draw and the geometry commands inside it, point constructors midpoint , foot , intersect , … , and symbol shortcuts - Hover information — a variable's value, or a built-in's math, keyword or geometry — including draw or constructor's description - Document symbols — jump to defines, variables, and draw blocks It works with .ezmath and .eml files. --- Running it From the project folder: The server communicates using standard JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout . Don't type into its terminal — your editor talks to it for you. > ⚠️ Logs and debugging go to stderr . Stdout is reserved for the > protocol and must not be polluted, or your editor will disconnect. --- Connecting your editor Any editor that can launch a custom stdio language server works. Two common setups: Neovim with nvim-lspconfig VS Code VS Code needs a small extension to launch a custom server. Options: 1. Use a generic LSP client extension e.g. "Generic LSP Client" from the marketplace configured with command uv run easy-math-lsp for the easymath language. 2. Associate the extension with .ezmath files first: "files.associations": { " .ezmath": "easymath" } . --- Troubleshooting | Problem | What to check | |---|---| | Editor says the server didn't start | Run uv run easy-math-lsp by hand and send it initialize — it should answer with its capabilities. Make sure uv sync was run so dependencies pygls are installed. | | No diagnostics appear | Confirm the file is recognized .ezmath / .eml extension or easymath language id and was opened after the server started. | | Server disconnects randomly | Something is writing to the server's stdout. Only stderr may be used for logs. | | Packaged app installer/ dist/ : editor can't start the server or compile | The editor finds easy-math-lsp / easy-math-lang next to itself the shared install folder without needing PATH . If you moved the binaries, keep them together or point EASYMATH_LSP_EXE / EASYMATH_COMPILER_EXE at the right files. | More editor and compiler problems: Troubleshooting and FAQ troubleshooting.md . --- For developers The server lives in src/lsp/ and reuses the compiler src/compiler/ , src/geometry/ instead of parsing the language a second time. title: Mod files (user commands)
text: Mod files user commands A mod file is a TOML file that adds math commands or overrides built-in ones. Load it from a document with: The path is relative to the .ezmath file's folder absolute paths are also allowed . The use line emits nothing in the output. All use lines are collected in a pre-pass, so their order does not matter; mod files load in the order the lines appear. Format Templates are Typst markup, not Python. A template must be a single math expression: it must start and end with $ and contain no and no inner $ . The compiler rejects anything else in a user mod. Mods cannot run Python; they can only shape output. Only load mods you trust — a mod can still consume compile time within the expansion budget and change the generated document. Each entry has name , args minimum argument count , usage and doc . An optional aliases array lists extra spellings. The typst template uses {0} , {1} , ... for the already-cleaned arguments; a literal brace is written as {{ or }} . Override rules - A template command may override a built-in template command; the compiler emits a warning command 'frac' overrides the built-in definition . - Overriding a built-in alias is allowed too overrides built-in alias 'fraction' of frac . - Overriding a command implemented in Python int , diff , cases , det , set , align , vec , matrix , pow , ... is an error and the entry is ignored. - Declaring kind = "builtin" or a handler key in a user mod is an error. - If two mod files define the same name, the later-loaded one wins and a warning names both files. Bad mod files Invalid TOML, missing args , a template referencing {3} with only 2 arguments, unknown keys, or duplicate names in one file produce diagnostics and never crash the build. A missing or unreadable mod file is an error at the use line. Editor and language server The language server loads mod files per document and includes their commands in completion and hover. Mod diagnostics appear on the use line. Editing a mod file on disk updates completions without reopening the document. The editor recompiles the preview on save; there is no file watcher for mod files.

title: Packaging and releases (for developers)
text: Packaging and releases for developers End users should start with the Installation guide installation.md . This page documents how the Windows/macOS installers and their binaries are built, how the editor finds them at runtime, and how to test all of it. <!-- toc --> - What gets built Windows what-gets-built-windows - Self-update on Windows how it avoids replacing a running app self-update-on-windows-how-it-avoids-replacing-a-running-app - The build scripts the-build-scripts - Binary size binary-size - What gets built macOS what-gets-built-macos - What gets built Linux what-gets-built-linux - What gets built Arch what-gets-built-arch - The release assets the-release-assets - Releasing releasing - Vendored Typst packages offline draw vendored-typst-packages-offline-draw - How it is wired how-it-is-wired - Updating the vendored packages updating-the-vendored-packages - Licensing licensing - How the editor finds its helpers at runtime how-the-editor-finds-its-helpers-at-runtime - Testing testing - Build performance build-performance <!-- /toc --> --- What gets built Windows Three PyInstaller binaries, with the exact flags used by CI scripts/build_binaries.py : | Binary | Mode | Contents | |---|---|---| | easy-math-lang/ shared bundle | onedir CLI | Compiler .ezmath → PDF/PNG/SVG/HTML/Typst via Typst | | ezmath | symlink / file copy | Short alias to the compiler POSIX: relative symlink; Windows: copy | | easy-math-lsp/ shared bundle | onedir CLI | Language server compiler bundled in-process | | easy-math-editor shared bundle | onedir GUI --windowed | Desktop editor PySide6 | All three executables are assembled into ONE shared bundle directory dist/easy-math-lang/ with a single _internal/ by scripts/build_binaries.py Approach A : the CLI and the language server reuse the desktop editor's collected libraries instead of each carrying their own copy, so an install holds exactly one copy of NumPy, Matplotlib, Typst, PySide6, … Inno Setup installer/setup.iss packs the shared bundle into EasyMathLang-Windows-x64-Setup.exe with this installed layout: The installer version comes from pyproject.toml — never hard-coded. CI reads it with tomllib the same source of truth as scripts/check_tag_version.py and passes it to ISCC as /DAppVersion=<version> ; setup.iss defines a 0.0.0 fallback under ifndef AppVersion so a hand-run ISCC.exe installer\setup.iss still compiles with a placeholder version instead of a stale one . tests/test_installer_script.py guards this statically. AppId is declared as exactly AppName no braces . Releases up to 7.0.0 shipped without an explicit AppId , so Inno used AppName as the implicit AppId and the uninstall key Easy Math Lang_is1 ; declaring anything else e.g. a braces literal would make new installers not see existing installs and leave two Add/Remove Programs entries behind. The CI job therefore installs the previous release first and then this build over it, and requires exactly one uninstall entry named Easy Math Lang else the build fails . When the previous release asset cannot be downloaded forks, or the first installer release , the step prints the manual procedure instead of verifying; run it by hand before tagging whenever it does — it installs into one shared directory and checks HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall for exactly one DisplayName = "Easy Math Lang" entry. Self-update on Windows how it avoids replacing a running app The helper that drives the Windows self-update is the CLI binary from the install directory, so it cannot stay running while the installer replaces that same binary and _internal/ . The flow is therefore: 1. The editor or easy-math-lang --update downloads the asset and SHA256SUMS.txt , and verifies SHA-256 and, immediately before the installer runs, again — see Security ../SECURITY.md updating--verification . 2. It spawns the helper easy-math-lang .exe --apply-update <plan> detached, then the editor quits through its normal shutdown path. 3. The helper waits for

title: The website
text: The website site/ holds the GitHub Pages site: a static landing page for easy-math-lang. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript — no framework, no build step, no external resources. The page is deployed by .github/workflows/pages.yml . One manual step is needed once: Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source: GitHub Actions . Regenerating the images Every image under site/assets/img/ is produced by the project itself — editor screenshots come from the real editor rendered offscreen, the example images come from the project compiler. Nothing is drawn by hand. The script - opens the real editor MainWindow , like the offscreen GUI tests do with examples/example_2.ezmath loaded and grabs it in English and Vietnamese, light and dark, plus the welcome banner and the draw gallery; - compiles the four built-in examples of src/editor/help_dialogs.py basic math, fraction/equation, vector, simple draw to SVG with compiler.pipeline.compile_ezmath and crops the page to its content; - writes site/assets/img/manifest.json with the SHA-256, the size and the way each image was produced. The output is deterministic: fixed window size, fixed theme, fixed example, an isolated settings file and no timestamps. Re-running the script on the same machine reproduces the same bytes. Checking the site It fails when a relative link or image does not resolve, when a data-i18n key is missing from en.json or vi.json , when an external http s resource would be loaded, when an image is not in the manifest or does not match its SHA-256, or is too small to be a real image , or when the site grows past 3 MB. The same checks run as part of the test suite tests/test_site.py . Translations site/i18n/en.json and site/i18n/vi.json hold the same keys. The English text is also in index.html , so the page stays readable when JavaScript is off. The Vietnamese strings reuse the wording of the editor's own catalog src/editor/locales/vi.json .

The Glossary glossary.md explains every word in plain language. --- First: how to read a message During a build you may see lines like this: - Line numbers count from the top of your .ezmath file. - Error — something is definitely wrong typo, bad calculation . - Warning — suspicious, but the build carries on. - Diagnostics print a small context block under their first line: the File "name", line N, column M header, the real .ezmath line, and a caret ^ under the exact spot. Columns count characters, not bytes Vietnamese text works the same , and tabs are expanded. When the column is not known there is no caret — you just get the file/line header and the source line. Very long lines are truncated around the caret with an ellipsis … . Almost every compiler diagnostic shows this block; the few that cannot point at a line in your file — CLI-level errors and Typst failures whose message carries no mappable position — keep the classic single-line output. - Color is only used on a terminal; when stderr is captured as in the editor or NO_COLOR is set, the output stays plain text. - Multi-line constructs point at the line where they open: an unclosed math delimiter \ … \ or an unterminated draw block is reported at the line with the opening delimiter. - By default the PDF is still written even with errors; the last line te
